summary: FQ-CoDel combines flow queueing with CoDel to fight bufferbloat. It mixes packets from many flows, limits head-of-line blocking from bursty traffic, and keeps low-rate traffic such as DNS from being stuck behind big transfers. This memo is Experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of one long line, each person gets their own mini-line and the cashier serves them in turn. A quick question is not stuck behind a huge order.

questions: how to reduce latency with fair queueing
subtitle: Fair queueing with active queue management to reduce latency and bufferbloat.

tldr.problem: Routers often buffer packets excessively, causing high latency and poor performance even when links have capacity. This 'bufferbloat' hurts interactive applications like video conferencing and web browsing.
tldr.mechanism: FQ-CoDel combines two techniques: flow queueing, which gives each flow its own queue to prevent one large transfer from blocking others, and CoDel (Controlled Delay), which drops packets when queues get too long to signal congestion early.
tldr.outcome: Connections experience lower latency and faster responsiveness without sacrificing link utilization, and the algorithm is lightweight enough for deployment in Linux kernel, home routers, and other hardware.

today: RFC 8290 is an Experimental specification that remains non-standard, but FQ-CoDel is widely deployed in Linux kernels and routers as the default queueing discipline, and has been extensively tested and proven effective at reducing bufferbloat.

sections.title: The Bufferbloat Problem
sections.content:
Routers and network devices buffer packets to smooth out traffic bursts, but excessive buffering creates high latency called bufferbloat. A single large file transfer can fill buffers and delay interactive traffic for seconds, hurting video calls, games, and web browsing. FQ-CoDel solves this by combining fair queueing with active queue management.

The algorithm is based on Deficit Round Robin (DRR) scheduling and the CoDel AQM algorithm. It is memory and CPU efficient, already shipping in the Linux kernel since version 3.5 and adopted as the default queueing discipline in distributions like OpenWrt, Arch Linux, and Fedora.
sections.plainLanguage: When networks get congested, buffers fill up and everything slows down. FQ-CoDel keeps buffers small and responsive by letting many flows share the queue fairly and dropping packets early when delays get too long.

sections.title: How FQ-CoDel Works
sections.content:
FQ-CoDel maintains multiple queues, by default 1024, each identified by a flow's 5-tuple: source and destination IP addresses, source and destination ports, and protocol number. Each flow is hashed into one of these buckets. Within each queue, CoDel controls delay: when packets have been sitting too long, CoDel drops them from the queue head, signaling congestion to the sender.

The scheduler uses a two-tier round-robin scheme with new and old queues. New queues (those that do not build up a standing queue) get priority, so short, bursty traffic like DNS queries and interactive traffic get through quickly. Once a queue empties, it drops back to new status for its next packet, providing implicit prioritization for low-volume flows.
sections.plainLanguage: FQ-CoDel sorts traffic by flow and manages how much each gets to send. It also drops packets when delays grow too long, telling senders to slow down before the buffer overflows.

sections.title: Tunable Parameters
sections.content:
FQ-CoDel exposes several parameters for configuration. The target parameter (default 5 ms) sets the acceptable minimum queue delay; the interval parameter (default 100 ms) is the time window for CoDel to detect persistent queue buildup. The quantum parameter (default 1514 bytes) controls how many bytes each queue gets per scheduling round. The limit parameter sets the hard packet limit per qdisc (default 10240 packets).

The number of flow buckets is set via the flows parameter (default 1024), which balances memory usage against hash collision probability. The noecn option disables Explicit Congestion Notification, and ce_threshold enables DCTCP-like behavior for low-latency data centers.
sections.plainLanguage: These knobs let network operators tune FQ-CoDel for their specific links, devices, and traffic patterns: slower links may need smaller buffers, busier networks may need more queues.

sections.title: Flow Isolation and Fairness
sections.content:
By isolating flows into separate queues, FQ-CoDel prevents head-of-line blocking: a bulk transfer cannot starve interactive traffic. However, the hashing approach is probabilistic—with 1024 buckets, a small number of flows may collide into the same queue. For up to 100 flows with 1024 buckets, the probability of no collisions is about 91%, and the probability that no more than two flows collide is 99.6%.

FQ-CoDel applies fairness at the flow level, not at other granularities. In some scenarios (ISP fairness between customers, transit provider fairness between ASes, or high-flow-count links), flow-level fairness may not be desired. The Linux implementation allows reconfiguring the classification scheme via the tc filter command to match on MAC addresses, Diffserv markings, or other packet fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Each flow gets fair access to the network, so a video stream does not starve your web browsing. But the fairness is probabilistic: some unrelated flows might accidentally end up in the same queue.

sections.title: Deployment and Results
sections.content:
FQ-CoDel has been included in the Linux kernel mainline since July 2012 (version 3.5), with Explicit Congestion Notification support added in version 4.2. Experimental data from Linux distributions, BSD implementations, and research show massive improvements in latency and fairness compared to the previous default FIFO queue. It is now the default queueing discipline in many Linux distributions.

Known limitations include difficulty with encrypted tunnels (opaque encapsulation bunches flows), challenges with low-priority delay-based congestion control algorithms (e.g., LEDBAT), and the need for tuning when fairness is desired at granularities other than flows. Future work includes the Cake algorithm, which extends FQ-CoDel principles with built-in rate limiting and improved hash collision handling.
sections.plainLanguage: FQ-CoDel is already built into many routers and Linux systems, and testing shows it massively improves responsiveness. The main challenge is tuning it for different networks and handling special cases.
